title: why some prayers need ten people
hookLine: why some prayers need ten people
tomorrow: the day the whole people says sorry together
last: GIVE BEFORE YOU FEEL LIKE IT.

cards: It's seven in the morning on a weekday, and a man is standing at the door of a small synagogue, looking up and down the street. Inside, eight people are waiting. He counts them again.
Eight, nine with him. Then a stranger walks past with a coffee, and the man calls out, a little embarrassed: excuse me, are you Jewish? Do you have ten minutes?
We need one more. In synagogues that are short a few people, scenes like this are part of the morning. Today: why some prayers can't be said until there are ten.

teach.b: A minyan is a count: ten adults, the smallest number Jewish law calls a community. A person can pray alone, anywhere, and Jews do. But certain prayers, the ones that speak as a public, need the ten.
The call to prayer, Barchu. The reading of the Torah from the scroll. And the Kaddish, including the mourner's Kaddish, said by someone who has lost a parent or a close relative.
Why ten? The rabbis found it in the Torah, in a roundabout way.
When twelve spies return from the promised land, ten of them bring back a frightening report, and God calls those ten a congregation. So the rabbis said: ten make a congregation.
Some teachers also point back to day eight, when Abraham bargained for Sodom and stopped at ten.
Who counts toward the ten is something Jews answer differently. In Orthodox communities, the minyan is ten men, thirteen and older: the age of bar mitzvah, from day six.
In Reform and Reconstructionist communities, and in egalitarian Conservative ones, women count equally. Now think about what the rule does for a mourner.

By custom, for eleven months after a parent dies, a traditional mourner says Kaddish every day. And because it needs a minyan, they can't say it alone. Every single day, nine other people have to show up, and answer amen.

The rule makes sure grief is never carried in an empty room. There's an old teaching that when ten gather to pray, the divine presence is among them. And the tenth person doesn't have to know the words.
Being there is what makes it count.

how: Jewish communities gather a minyan of ten for daily and Sabbath services so that the Torah can be read and Barchu and Kaddish said; Orthodox communities count ten men, while Reform, Reconstructionist and egalitarian Conservative communities count women and men alike.

games.q: your father has died, and you want to say the mourner's Kaddish every morning. what do you need?
games.why: nine others, to make ten. every day, the community has to show up so grief is never carried alone.

practice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Count your own minyan. Think of the people who would show up if you called: at a hospital, at a funeral, at a table.
Name them in your head, one at a time, and see how far you get. Ten, or three, or one. Then think of someone who might not reach ten, and whose count you could join.

wordCard.voice: Minyan. A count of ten, the smallest community, so some prayers are never said alone. Seventeenth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a count, a number, from a root meaning to count.
